slides.heading: Year 1 — Autumn 2, Week 4
slides.sub: New content taught directly, practised in words/sentences and applied in reading and dictation.

slides.heading: Mon
slides.objective: Learn the new sound "o-e" (/əʊ/) and start reading and spelling words that use it.

slides.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="320" height="320" role="img" aria-label="nose" class="wp-icon wp-raster" data-picture="nose_icon"><image href="data:image/png;base64," x="0" y="0" width="100" height="100" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"/></svg>

slides.mnemonic: Hollow the Nest sits snug at the end of the word, and she calls softly back over the consonant so the 'o' at the front says its own name, 'oh', like calling everyone home.

character.name: Hollow the Nest
character.blurb: Hollow the Nest is a cosy little nest lined with one soft tuft of moss, and she calls back across the word to bring the 'o' safely home.

slides.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oa' in boat and 'oe' in toe — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
slides.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'o', then a consonant, then 'e' at the end — like home, where 'o' and 'e' sit either side of the middle letter like two ends of the same nest.
slides.action: Children cup both hands together like a little nest, then slowly pull them apart while saying 'oh', as if opening the nest to let the sound out.
slides.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="320" height="320" role="img" aria-label="nose" class="wp-icon wp-raster" data-picture="nose_icon"><image href="data:image/png;base64," x="0" y="0" width="100" height="100" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"/></svg>

slides.tip: The 'o' says /u/ and the 'e' on the end is silent — it rhymes with 'glove' and 'dove', not with 'move'.

slides.heading: Tue
slides.objective: Learn the new sound "u-e" (/juː/) and start reading and spelling words that use it.

slides.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-90 -110 180 180" width="320" height="320" role="img" aria-label="ice cube" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" class="wp-icon" data-picture="ice_cube"><rect x="-45" y="-56" width="90" height="56" rx="6" ry="6" fill="#c3ced6" stroke="#3b4954" stroke-width="3.5"/><rect x="-59" y="-39.2" width="14" height="10" rx="6" ry="6" fill="#c3ced6" stroke="#3b4954" stroke-width="2.5"/><rect x="45" y="-39.2" width="14" height="10" rx="6" ry="6" fill="#c3ced6" stroke="#3b4954" stroke-width="2.5"/><ellipse cx="0" cy="-56" rx="45" ry="8" fill="#c3ced6" stroke="#3b4954" stroke-width="2.5"/></svg>

slides.mnemonic: Tuney Bee hums her favourite tune at the end of the word, sending her buzz back over the consonant so the 'u' at the front wakes up and says its own name, 'you'.

character.name: Tuney Bee
character.blurb: Tuney Bee has berry-dark stripes and loves to hum, sending her buzzing sound back across the word to wake the 'u' at the front.

slides.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oo' in moon (and sometimes sounds like 'you', as in cube) — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
slides.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'u', then a consonant, then 'e' at the end — like cube, where 'u' and 'e' sit either side of the middle letter like two ends of the same tune.
slides.action: Children cup a hand behind their ear as if listening for a tune, then hum 'u' softly while bringing the hand forward.
